cues.text: Let us turn now to the second major part of this study session: change models.
Whenever an organisation undertakes digital transformation, it is asking people to work differently.
New systems, new data, new processes, all of these only create value if people actually adopt them.
So we need structured ways of thinking about how change happens, and we will look at three of them.
We begin with the best known of these, Kotter's eight steps.
Kotter's model describes change as a sequence of eight steps.
The source sets these out in a table with three columns.
The first column is Step, the second is Meaning, and the third is Example.
Let us walk through it row by row, in order.
Step one is create urgency.
Its meaning is to explain why change is necessary now.
The example given is to show increasing service delays and customer loss.
Think about why this comes first.
People rarely give up familiar routines unless they believe staying the same is risky.
So leaders must make the case, with evidence such as growing delays and customers leaving, that the present way of working cannot continue.
Step two is build a guiding coalition.
The meaning is to form an influential, cross-functional leadership group.
The example is product, IT, operations and compliance sponsors.
Notice the word cross-functional.
A digital change touches many departments, so the people leading it must come from several of them, and they must have real influence.
One enthusiastic department cannot carry the whole organisation.
Step three is form vision and strategy.
The meaning is to define the future state and the direction.
The example is a reliable, accessible digital service.
The vision answers the question, what are we trying to become?
The strategy then explains how we will get there.
Step four is communicate and enlist support.
The meaning is to mobilise understanding and participation.
The examples are team meetings, demonstrations, often called demos, and dialogue.
Observe that this step is not one announcement.
It involves showing people the new approach and listening to them, so that they understand it and take part.
Step five is remove barriers.
The meaning is to empower people and resolve obstacles.
The examples are training, simplified approvals and tools.
If people are enthusiastic but lack skills, face slow approval chains, or have no proper tools, the change stalls.
This step clears those obstacles.
Step six is generate short-term wins.
The meaning is to deliver visible, credible benefits.
The example is a successful pilot that reduces wait times.
A pilot is a small-scale trial.
When people see waiting times fall, they gain confidence that the change works.
Step seven is sustain acceleration.
The meaning is to build on the wins and tackle the remaining issues.
The examples are to expand the rollout and improve processes.
Early success is used as momentum, not as a reason to stop.
Step eight is anchor change.
The meaning is to embed new behaviours in culture and systems.
The examples are updated roles, rewards and procedures.
Change becomes lasting only when job descriptions, incentives and standard procedures reflect the new way of working, so that people do not slide back to old habits.
Now the source adds some important qualifications.
Classic and newer formulations of Kotter's model use slightly different labels.
But the underlying sequence is the same: urgency, coalition, vision, mobilisation, barrier removal, wins, acceleration and institutionalisation.
Institutionalisation simply means making the change a normal, built-in part of the organisation, which matches step eight.
Also, steps can overlap in practice.
You do not always finish one completely before beginning the next.
And one warning deserves emphasis: do not confuse short-term wins with final completion.
A successful pilot at step six is encouraging, but the work continues through steps seven and eight.
The second model is Lewin's model.
It has three phases.
First, unfreeze existing habits.
This means loosening the current ways of working so that people become open to something different.
Second, change through transition and new behaviours.
This is the period in which people actually try and learn the new ways.
Third, refreeze by reinforcing the new state.
The source clarifies that refreezing means stabilising valuable practices, not banning future learning.
So the goal is to make good new practices steady, while the organisation remains free to keep learning and improving.
The third model is ADKAR, and it differs in focus, because it concerns individual adoption.
The letters stand for five elements.
A is Awareness, which answers why the change is needed.
D is Desire, meaning willingness to take part.
K is Knowledge, meaning how to do it.
A, the second one, is Ability, meaning demonstrated capability, that is, the person can actually perform the new way of working.
And R is Reinforcement, meaning what sustains the change over time.
The source gives a useful caution: a worker may know how to use a tool but lack desire or opportunity, so training alone may not solve the problem.
Knowledge is only one element.
The lesson is to diagnose the specific barrier.
Is the person unaware, unwilling, untrained, unable, or unsupported afterwards?
The remedy should match the real gap.
Finally, the source compares the three models.
Kotter emphasises organisational mobilisation, that is, getting the whole organisation moving.
Lewin explains the broad transition phases, the overall shape of moving from old to new.
ADKAR diagnoses individual adoption, helping us see where one person is stuck.
They can be used together when appropriate.

And the source closes with a point that matters for digital transformation in particular: it can require iterative changes, meaning repeated cycles of change, rather than a single linear programme that runs once from start to finish.
